newsitem.title: BELGIUM: BELGIUM AIMS TO "COOK BOOKS" PERMANENTLY FOR EMU.
newsitem.headline: BELGIUM AIMS TO "COOK BOOKS" PERMANENTLY FOR EMU.

text.p: Belgium proposed on Friday a new law obliging around 100 semi-governmental social security and other funds to place excess liquidities in government debt, thereby helping its case for economic and monetary union (EMU).

Under the Maastricht Treaty, any public debt instruments held by quasi non-governmental organisations (quangos) counts as a state asset, thereby reducing a country's net debt position as defined for EMU.

Belgium has the highest debt of any European Union country. At around 129 percent of gross domestic product it is well above the Maastricht reference level of 60 percent, although the debt is declining as a percentage of GDP.

When it emerged earlier this year that Belgium had already informal arrangements with the funds concerning their debt placements the country was accused of "cooking its books" for EMU -- a charge which the finance ministry angrily denied.
An article in the Wall Street Journal Europe claimed that many of the placements were made for only a few days over the New Year period when end-of-year accounts are drawn up.
In 1996 the estimated impact of such measures was to reduce Belgium's debt by around 80 billion Belgian francs.
"With this law we want to show everyone that we are doing things according to the book -- the rules of Maastricht -- nothing more and nothing less," a finance ministry official told Reuters.
The plans have already been approved by the European Union's statistical office Eurostat, he noted.

The new law amends existing rules covering the social security sector dating from 1954 under which the funds were obliged to hold their liquidities in public debt or state-owned banks, most of which have since been privatised.
The finance ministry official said, however, it had been found that not all funds that exist today were covered by the 1954 law - a plug hole which the new legislation will fill.

"Most of the (100) funds, around 80 or 90, already fell under the 1954 law and just a small percentage of reserves was allowed to be invested in another form," he added. "This means the impact of the new law will be quite small."

The funds covered by the new legislation range from the state pension fund, which at certain times of the year contains billions of francs, down to funds linked to the royal museums, which manage only a few millions, he said.
Estimating the total amount of funds affected by the legislation was impossible because it varied during the year according to the calendar of payments the social security bodies had to respect.

In future, the legislation could also be extended to the semi-public institutions that are responsible for dispersing the social security funds to the public, something which often takes place by a network of so-called "mutuelles" or "mutualiteiten".

"The proposal is such that in future we can direct all organisations forming missions of a public interest, especially in the social security sector...to put more reserves in such a mechanism," the official said.
He noted that many of the bodies concerned had benefited for years from favourable tax treatment by the government.
